title: Linear Algebra Lecture 7: Eigenvectors, Eigenvalues and Diagonalization
description: Lecture 7 of an undergraduate linear algebra course: eigenvectors as invariant directions, computing eigenvalues from the characteristic polynomial, diagonalization, and when it fails. Recorded in a temporary room with a faulty clip-on mic, so apologies for the audio. Written notes are on the course page.

segments.text: Okay, can everyone in the back hear me?
Sorry about the echo in this room, the usual lecture hall was booked, and the clip-on microphone keeps cutting out,
so if the recording sounds rough, that's why. The board should still be readable.
Today is lecture seven, and the topic is eigenvectors and eigenvalues.
I want to start not with the definition but with a picture.
Take a matrix, any two by two matrix, and think of it as a machine that moves every point in the plane.
Most vectors get knocked off their line.
You feed in a vector pointing northeast and it comes out pointing somewhere else entirely.
But for many matrices there are a few special directions where that doesn't happen.
A vector on that line comes out on the same line, only stretched, or shrunk, or flipped.
Those directions are the eigenvectors, and the stretch factor is the eigenvalue.
Written as an equation, A times v equals lambda times v.
The matrix acting on v does nothing more than scale it. Let's do an example on the board.
Take A equal to the matrix with rows two, one and one, two.
To find the eigenvalues, we want a nonzero v with A minus lambda I, times v, equal to zero.
A nonzero vector in the null space means A minus lambda I is singular, which means its determinant is zero.
So we compute two minus lambda, squared, minus one, equals zero.
Expand that and you get lambda squared minus four lambda plus three, which factors as lambda minus one times lambda minus three.
Eigenvalues one and three. Now plug each one back in.
For lambda equals three, A minus three I has rows minus one, one and one, minus one, so the null space is spanned by one,
one. For lambda equals one, A minus I has rows one, one and one, one, so we get one, minus one.
Notice something. Those two eigenvectors are perpendicular. That's not a coincidence.
Our matrix is symmetric, and the spectral theorem says a real symmetric matrix always has real eigenvalues and an orthogonal set of eigenvectors.
We'll prove that next week. Here's why this matters. In the eigenvector basis, the matrix is just diagonal.
Along the one, one direction it multiplies by three, and along the one, minus one direction it multiplies by one.
So if I ask you for A to the tenth power, you don't multiply ten matrices.
You write your vector in the eigenbasis and raise each eigenvalue to the tenth.
Three to the tenth and one to the tenth. That's the whole idea behind diagonalization.
A equals P D P inverse, and A to the k equals P D to the k P inverse.
A quick warning, because this trips people up on the exam every year. Not every matrix is diagonalizable.
Take the shear matrix with rows one, one and zero, one.
Its only eigenvalue is one, repeated, but it only has one independent eigenvector.
You can't build a basis out of eigenvectors, so diagonalization fails. The algebraic multiplicity is two, the geometric multiplicity is one.
Also, a rotation of the plane by ninety degrees has no real eigenvectors at all, because every vector gets turned.
Its eigenvalues are i and minus i. Complex eigenvalues are the algebra's way of telling you there's rotation going on.
Sorry, the mic just clipped again, let me repeat that. Complex eigenvalues signal rotation.
Last thing, a connection to where you'll actually see this.
If you have a system that evolves step by step, like a population model where x next equals A times x,
then the long-run behaviour is controlled by the eigenvalue with the largest absolute value. If it's bigger than one, things grow.
If it's less than one, they decay. And the corresponding eigenvector tells you the shape the system settles into.
Ranking pages by the links between them can be phrased exactly this way, as finding a dominant eigenvector.
For homework, problems four through nine in section six point one, and please try the shear example by hand before Thursday.
And if the audio on this recording is unusable, the written notes are posted on the course page. See you Thursday.
